Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love quite like the release of a caged butterfly, does it?

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are reportedly set to receive $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are said to be the pièce de résistance of England’s most eagerly anticipated celebrity wedding of the year.

The gesture has been widely pilloried in the British media, with many dismissing it as tacky and excessive. But is that criticism merely sour grapes?

It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road to the altar for the couple—one strewn with fierce criticism from a British press that has seemed to relish lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin as “common.” The Daily Mail once even asked: “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Rooney has been dubbed “Shrek” and “Mr. Potato Head” because of his looks, while his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often invoked in a disparaging manner. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page after page of scathing stories about her weight, her shopping sprees, and her apparent lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham.

There has also been fierce criticism of the fact that she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. Apparently, it is all down to Rooney—and nothing to do with her seeming to be quite a decent person, someone who did well at school and has shrewdly parlayed some of her fame into various media and advertising projects.

Anyone who has seen her television show, *Coleen’s Real Women*, can see that she is a decent, bubbly person who is particularly good at putting others at ease.

Much to the media’s fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover their wedding to *OK!* magazine for a record $5 million. However, they are not keeping all the money for themselves: an undisclosed sum from the fee is to be donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, is cared for.

The Queen’s grandson, Peter Phillips, and his bride, Autumn Kelly, recently received $1 million from *Hello!* magazine to cover their wedding, yet they did not attract even an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous—but lower-class—Rooney and McLoughlin.

The wedding may be extravagant, complete with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests—whose costs the couple are covering—along with expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress. But at least Rooney and McLoughlin have worked hard for what they have.

Their success despite their working-class backgrounds appears to be the greatest source of frustration for their critics. It seems simply unacceptable to some that people who were not born into privilege and did not attend elite schools should enjoy their wealth. That, apparently, would be ugly.

If anything, the couple’s relationship and success represent a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, though she spent two years fending off Rooney’s entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, asked her again, and this time received a yes.

Surely they deserve congratulations for creating their own modern fairy tale—complete with butterflies?

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

LONDON, England (CNN) — What could be a better symbol of romance than setting butterflies free from boxes?

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are reportedly receiving $5 million for the photographic rights to their wedding. The butterfly release is said to be the showpiece of what has been described as England’s most eagerly awaited celebrity wedding of the year.

Rooney, widely regarded as the finest English footballer of his generation, and McLoughlin, his school-days sweetheart, were due to marry on Thursday in Italy in a ceremony estimated to cost $10 million. According to reports, guests were expected to open boxes and release butterflies as the couple kissed.

That planned gesture has been mocked heavily in the British press, where many commentators have dismissed it as tasteless and excessive. But is the criticism really just envy?

The couple’s journey to marriage has been lengthy and, at times, difficult. Along the way, they have endured harsh attacks from sections of the British media, which has often seemed to take pleasure in ridiculing Rooney and McLoughlin as “common.” The Daily Mail once went so far as to ask: “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Rooney has been nicknamed “Shrek” and “Mr Potato Head” because of his appearance. His upbringing — as the son of a school dinner lady and as someone raised on a council estate — is frequently mentioned in a sneering tone.

McLoughlin, for her part, has faced endless hostile coverage about her weight, her shopping habits and her supposed lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. She has also been strongly criticized for becoming a millionaire in her own right.

Apparently, her success is all because of Rooney, rather than anything to do with the possibility that she is a genuinely pleasant person, someone who did well academically and has smartly turned part of her fame into television, media and advertising work.

Anyone who has watched her program, *Coleen’s Real Women*, can see that she comes across as warm, lively and skilled at making others feel comfortable.

To the irritation of the media, the couple sold coverage rights for the wedding to *OK!* magazine for a record $5 million. But they are not keeping the whole amount. An unspecified portion of the money is to be donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, receives care.

Recently, the queen’s grandson Peter Phillips and his wife Autumn Kelly were paid $1 million by *Hello!* magazine for coverage of their wedding. Yet they did not face anything close to the level of condemnation now being aimed at Rooney and McLoughlin, who are giving away more but are seen as belonging to a lower social class.

In addition, instead of wedding gifts, Rooney and McLoughlin have asked their guests to contribute money to Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool.

The wedding may well be extravagant, with a private yacht, a luxury jet for guests — whose expenses the couple are paying — costly wine and a wedding dress worth $200,000. Still, Rooney and McLoughlin have earned what they have through their own efforts.

For many critics, the most galling thing seems to be that the couple have achieved success despite coming from working-class backgrounds. The idea that people who were not born into privilege and did not attend elite schools might enjoy their wealth appears to be considered unacceptable.

That, surely, is the uglier attitude.

If anything, Rooney and McLoughlin’s relationship and achievements should be seen as a victory over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, though she spent two years turning down Rooney’s requests for a date.

He eventually got his opportunity when he spotted her trying to repair a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help her, asked her out again, and this time she said yes.

Surely they deserve some credit for building their own modern fairy tale — butterflies included.

The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding in Italy was always going to attract attention. Rooney was one of England’s most famous footballers, McLoughlin was already a celebrity in her own right, and the pair had grown up in public from teenage sweethearts into a wealthy, heavily photographed couple. Their marriage was not simply treated as a private celebration, but as a national media event: a lavish ceremony abroad, designer clothes, luxury hotels, celebrity guests, and a reported $5 million deal for the photographic rights. Even the planned release of butterflies became a symbol in the press of what many commentators portrayed as extravagance pushed into absurdity.

But the reaction to the wedding revealed as much about the British media as it did about Rooney and McLoughlin. Much of the coverage was not merely curious or amused; it was openly contemptuous. Newspapers and columnists mocked the couple’s taste, their spending, their accents, their clothes, and their supposedly “common” idea of glamour. The wedding was described as excessive, vulgar, and tacky, as though the couple had committed some kind of cultural offence by enjoying the wealth their fame had brought them. Beneath the jokes about butterflies and photo deals lay a familiar form of class judgment: the suggestion that money earned by working-class celebrities is somehow less respectable than inherited privilege or wealth displayed by people with the “right” background.

Rooney and McLoughlin were easy targets because they did not fit the traditional image of elegance preferred by certain sections of the press. They were young, rich, northern, and unashamedly visible. Their fame came not from aristocratic lineage or elite education, but from football, fashion, tabloid culture, and popular fascination. To critics, this made them symbols of a celebrity age in which money and publicity appeared to replace refinement. Yet that criticism often seemed less like a principled objection to extravagance and more like snobbery dressed up as cultural commentary.

After all, lavish weddings are hardly unusual among the wealthy. The British establishment has long celebrated grand ceremonies, exclusive venues, designer gowns, and expensive displays of status. When similar extravagance is attached to royalty, aristocracy, or old money, it is often presented as tradition, romance, or national spectacle. When it is attached to a footballer from Croxteth and his childhood sweetheart, it is more likely to be called vulgar. The difference lies not in the spending itself, but in who is doing the spending and whether the media believes they have the social permission to do it.

The photo-rights deal also became part of the criticism. Selling wedding photographs for millions was portrayed as evidence of greed or shameless self-promotion. Yet celebrity magazines and newspapers were themselves competing to profit from public interest in the couple. The media condemned the commercialisation of the wedding while simultaneously feeding the market that made such a deal possible. Rooney and McLoughlin were not inventing celebrity culture; they were participating in a system built and sustained by the very outlets that mocked them.

Their popularity complicates the sneering tone of the coverage. However much commentators derided them, the public remained interested in their lives. Rooney’s success on the football pitch gave him a kind of national significance, while McLoughlin’s style, relationships, and personal story attracted a large audience. They represented a version of aspiration that many people recognised: ordinary beginnings, sudden wealth, family loyalty, and the desire to enjoy success openly rather than quietly. The wedding’s extravagance may have seemed excessive to some, but it also reflected a fantasy of achievement and celebration that celebrity culture encourages.

This is why the backlash against the wedding seems rooted less in genuine moral concern than in class prejudice and jealousy. The couple were mocked not simply because they spent money, but because they were seen as spending it incorrectly. They were accused of lacking taste by commentators who often equate taste with class background. Their happiness was treated as comic material, their success as suspicious, and their glamour as illegitimate. The language used against them—“tacky,” “common,” “vulgar”—carried a social meaning that went far beyond criticism of one wedding.

In the end, Rooney and McLoughlin’s Italian wedding became a stage on which British anxieties about class, money, fame, and taste were acted out. The butterflies, the magazine deal, and the luxury setting were only the surface details. The deeper story was the discomfort caused when people from ordinary backgrounds became rich enough and famous enough to command the kind of attention once reserved for elites. The mockery directed at them said less about their character than about a media culture eager to police the boundaries of respectability. Far from proving that the couple were ridiculous, the reaction exposed the snobbery of those determined to ridicule them.

counterfactuals.output:
**Opinion: Let Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin have their fairy-tale wedding**

The British press has long had a peculiar talent for turning a young working-class success story into a national morality play. So it was almost inevitable that Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding would be treated not simply as a private celebration, but as evidence to be mocked, judged and picked apart.

Yes, the wedding was extravagant. There was an Italian Riviera setting, designer clothes, celebrity guests and the now-famous release of butterflies — the sort of detail practically designed to send tabloid columnists into a state of performative outrage. And yes, the couple reportedly agreed a lucrative photo deal with *OK!* magazine. But the fury directed at them says less about Rooney and McLoughlin than it does about Britain’s enduring discomfort with working-class people spending money in public.

There is a familiar double standard at work. When aristocrats, financiers or old-money celebrities stage elaborate weddings, the spectacle is often framed as tradition, glamour or heritage. When a young footballer from Liverpool and his childhood sweetheart do it, it is more likely to be called tasteless, vulgar or excessive. The spending itself is not really the issue. The issue is who is doing the spending.

Rooney’s wealth did not arrive through inheritance or social connections. It came through extraordinary talent, pressure and scrutiny from a very young age. McLoughlin, too, had been turned into a public figure before she had much chance to choose the terms of that attention. If they wanted to mark their wedding with grandeur, why should that be considered uniquely offensive?

The *OK!* magazine deal has also been treated as proof of commercialism. But celebrity media arrangements are hardly new, and they can serve a practical purpose: controlling access, limiting paparazzi chaos and ensuring that one approved set of images is published rather than allowing a free-for-all. For a couple who had grown up under relentless media attention, selling official photos was not necessarily cynical. It may simply have been sensible.

Nor should the criticism ignore the fact that charitable donations were reportedly connected to the wedding coverage. If a media deal turns public curiosity into money that can benefit good causes, that complicates the lazy narrative of pure self-indulgence. It is strange to condemn a couple both for profiting from attention and for channeling some of that money toward charity.

As for the butterflies, they have become an easy punchline — a symbol, critics suggest, of excess. But weddings are full of symbolic gestures: doves, fireworks, horse-drawn carriages, ice sculptures, designer flowers. The butterfly release was memorable because it sounded fanciful and expensive, but fanciful gestures are hardly unusual at weddings. They are, in many ways, the point.

What seems to irritate critics most is not that Rooney and McLoughlin celebrated love, success and family, but that they did so without apologizing for it. Their wedding did not conform to the restrained, tasteful aesthetic preferred by commentators who often mistake their own class codes for universal standards of dignity.

There is nothing wrong with questioning celebrity excess in a world of inequality. But that critique should be consistent. Too often, British media scorn falls hardest on those who have escaped modest beginnings and dare to enjoy the rewards. The message is unmistakable: success is acceptable, provided you spend it quietly, deferentially and in ways approved by people who never had to fight for entry into elite spaces.

Rooney and McLoughlin’s wedding may not have been everyone’s idea of elegance. It did not have to be. It was their wedding, their money, their moment. Behind the mockery lies an old prejudice dressed up as good taste — and that is far more unappealing than a few butterflies on the Italian coast.

## The Rooney Wedding Backlash Was Never Really About the Money

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin married in a lavish celebrity wedding, the reaction was as predictable as it was revealing. There were headlines about extravagance, tutting over the price tag, mockery of the outfits, the guests, the setting, the taste. The implication was clear: this was not simply a young couple spending a fortune on their wedding. It was a young working-class couple spending a fortune — and enjoying it too visibly.

That distinction matters.

Britain has always had an uneasy relationship with wealth, but it is far more forgiving when money comes wrapped in the right accent, the right schooling and the right kind of understatement. Aristocratic excess is often treated as heritage. City wealth can be reframed as ambition. Old money gets called tradition. But when newly rich people from working-class backgrounds spend conspicuously, the language changes. Suddenly it becomes “vulgar,” “tacky,” “bling,” “too much.”

The backlash against Rooney and McLoughlin’s wedding sat squarely in that tradition. Of course, the event was extravagant. Celebrity weddings usually are. Footballers, pop stars, actors and heiresses have long turned private milestones into public spectacles. But the intensity of the criticism aimed at the Rooneys seemed less about the existence of excess than about who was indulging in it.

Wayne Rooney was not a polished society figure. He was a prodigiously talented footballer from Croxteth, a player whose gifts had lifted him from a working-class Liverpool upbringing into extraordinary wealth. Coleen McLoughlin, his childhood sweetheart, became famous not through aristocratic lineage or media training but by proximity to football culture and tabloid fascination. They were young, rich and unmistakably ordinary in origin. That combination has always irritated a certain section of British public life.

The complaints about “waste” might have sounded more convincing if such moral outrage were applied evenly. But it rarely is. The weddings of the wealthy and well-connected have long been treated as occasions of glamour, aspiration or national curiosity. When the upper classes stage grand ceremonies in stately homes, with couture dresses, rare flowers and guest lists full of titled acquaintances, the coverage tends to be admiring. When footballers do something similar, it is often framed as a lapse in taste.

This is not to say that criticism of celebrity extravagance is never legitimate. In a country marked by inequality, there is always something uncomfortable about displays of extreme wealth. Weddings costing millions can feel jarringly out of step with ordinary life. But if the objection is truly economic, it should apply to all excessive displays of privilege — not just those performed by people who sound like they came from the terraces rather than the drawing room.

What made the Rooney-McLoughlin reaction so telling was the language of contempt. The issue was not merely that they had spent too much. It was that they had spent too much in the “wrong” way. Their taste was scrutinised as though it were a moral failing. Their background was never far from the subtext. They had money, but not the cultural permission that often comes with inherited status.

There is an old British anxiety at work here: the fear of social mobility when it becomes visible. We claim to celebrate people who rise from humble beginnings, but only if they adopt the manners of those already at the top. The working-class success story is applauded when it is humble, grateful and restrained. It becomes offensive when it is loud, glamorous or self-confident.

Rooney’s career was built on talent of a kind that could not be inherited or faked. He earned his fortune in one of the few industries where working-class boys have historically been able to become genuinely rich through exceptional ability. Yet football wealth is often treated as less legitimate than wealth acquired through finance, property or family inheritance. The footballer is expected to apologise for his money in a way the landowner rarely is.

Coleen, too, became a particular target of class-coded criticism. Like many women attached to famous men, she was judged not only for what she did but for what she was perceived to represent. Her clothes, choices and public image were dissected with a disdain that often revealed more about the critics than the subject. She was mocked for enjoying the lifestyle that fame and wealth had brought, as though enjoyment itself were unbecoming.

The wedding therefore became a cultural Rorschach test. To some, it was simply a big celebrity event. To others, it was evidence of excess. But to many commentators, consciously or not, it appeared to symbolise something more troubling: people from the “wrong” side of the class divide refusing to stay modest.

That is why the charge of vulgarity deserves scrutiny. “Vulgar” is one of those words Britain often uses when it wants to talk about class without admitting it. It masquerades as aesthetic judgment, but it frequently carries a social one. It suggests not just that something is unattractive, but that the people responsible do not know their place.

The Rooneys’ wedding may not have been to everyone’s taste. It did not need to be. Weddings are personal, even when they become public spectacles. But the ferocity of the backlash tells us less about one couple’s spending habits than about Britain’s lingering discomfort with working-class people acquiring wealth and displaying it on their own terms.

If extravagance is the problem, then let us be consistent. Criticise all obscene concentrations of wealth. Question all industries that turn private life into marketable spectacle. Challenge the broader culture that equates love, success and status with cost. But do not pretend that a footballer’s wedding is uniquely offensive while treating upper-class opulence as charming tradition.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding was certainly lavish. It may even have been excessive. But the sneering response was about more than extravagance. It was about class, taste and the unwritten rules of British respectability. The real offence, for some, was not that they spent too much. It was that they were working-class people who had made money — and dared to celebrate like they belonged.

When one of England’s most famous footballers marries his childhood sweetheart in a reported $10 million ceremony, complete with exclusive picture rights said to be worth around $5 million, the event becomes a national talking point — part romance, part spectacle, part media circus.

And that is exactly what happened.

To some, the Rooneys’ wedding was an extravagant fairytale: two teenagers from Liverpool who grew up together, survived the pressures of fame, money and tabloid scrutiny, and finally married in front of family and friends. Their story has long carried the appeal of a modern working-class romance — childhood sweethearts from Croxteth who found themselves catapulted into the strange, glittering world of Premier League celebrity.

To others, the wedding was an easy target. Reports of luxury venues, designer details and dramatic flourishes — including the much-discussed release of butterflies — invited mockery from newspapers, columnists and online commentators. In Britain, where footballers’ wealth is often viewed with a mix of fascination and resentment, a multimillion-dollar wedding is practically a provocation. The public may love a rags-to-riches story, but it also enjoys puncturing one.

The reported $5 million magazine deal for exclusive photographs added another layer. Critics saw it as evidence of celebrity excess: a private milestone converted into a commercial event. Yet that criticism is not entirely fair. In the modern celebrity economy, privacy is often less something stars possess than something they negotiate. If photographers are going to chase the images anyway, selling controlled access can be seen as pragmatic rather than crass.

There was also a charitable dimension that complicated the caricature. The couple reportedly directed proceeds from the picture deal toward charity, a detail often mentioned after the jokes had already landed. It may not silence every criticism — extravagance and generosity can coexist uneasily — but it does challenge the simplest version of the story: that the wedding was only about vanity and display.

The butterflies became the perfect symbol of the public reaction. Intended, presumably, as romantic and delicate, they were treated by sections of the press as comic proof of over-the-top taste. But celebrity weddings are rarely judged on their own terms. They become mirrors for whatever the audience already believes: that footballers are vulgar, that young wealth is tasteless, that tabloid culture is exploitative, or that romance still matters even when surrounded by cameras.

What makes Rooney and Coleen’s wedding endure as a subject of interest is not merely the money. It is the contrast. At the center of all the extravagance was a relationship that began long before the contracts, mansions, magazine covers and England caps. Their childhood romance gave the wedding an emotional authenticity that could not be bought, even if nearly everything around it appeared to have a price tag.

In that sense, the spectacle was almost beside the point. The Rooneys’ wedding was mocked because it was huge, photographed because it was valuable, and debated because it sat at the intersection of fame, class and money in modern Britain. But beneath the butterflies and the headlines was a simpler story: two people who knew each other before the world knew them, trying — however publicly — to turn a teenage romance into a lifelong commitment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an editorial in the voice of a sympathetic British columnist about Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin getting married in Italy, defending them from tabloid attacks and framing their success as a modern fairytale.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Modern Fairytale, Whether the Snobs Like It or Not**

There is something faintly ridiculous about the national habit of pretending we are above celebrity weddings while devouring every detail of them over breakfast. So it is with Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin, whose marriage in Italy has been greeted in some quarters not with simple good wishes, but with the usual chorus of sneers: too lavish, too gaudy, too much security, too much money, too young, too famous, too everything.

One wonders what, precisely, the couple were meant to do. Marry in a municipal office under flickering fluorescent lights, issue a statement of apology for their bank balance, and promise never again to enjoy the fruits of their extraordinary ascent? The criticism says rather less about them than it does about a peculiar British discomfort with people from ordinary backgrounds having the nerve to succeed visibly.

Because that, at the heart of it, is the story. Strip away the flashbulbs, the designer gowns, the Italian scenery and the feverish tabloid arithmetic, and you find two young people who have known each other since childhood, who grew up in the same world long before the world came banging at their door. They are not aristocrats consolidating estates, nor dynasts merging fortunes. They are a boy from Croxteth and the girl who knew him before the goals, before the contracts, before the headlines, before the country decided it owned a share in him.

That is why the mockery feels so sour. Wayne Rooney’s gifts made him famous while he was still barely more than a child. Coleen, too, was thrust into a strange half-life in which every handbag, holiday and haircut became material for public judgment. They have grown up not merely in public, but under inspection. Every mistake inflated, every purchase moralised, every private milestone turned into a national referendum on taste.

And now they have married — in Italy, no less — and the tutting begins again. But Italy has always been a place where romance is permitted to be theatrical. If a young couple with the means to do so choose sunshine, family, friends and a little splendour, why should that offend us? We do not demand austerity from dukes, discretion from hedge-fund men, or modesty from the genuinely grand. It is only when working-class success becomes decorative that the finger-wagging starts.

There is a class story here, though many will pretend otherwise. Footballers occupy a curious place in British life: adored on Saturday, resented by Sunday. We cheer the goals, then bridle at the wages. We ask them to carry our hopes and then scold them for buying nice things with the money we helped pour into the game. Rooney, with his blunt brilliance and unmistakably ordinary origins, has never been an easy fit for those who prefer their sporting heroes polished, media-trained and apologetically grateful.

Coleen has faced her own version of the same snobbery. She has been described endlessly through the language of consumption, as though a young woman’s shopping habits were a matter of national consequence. Yet there has always been something admirably steady about her. She has navigated a life of sudden wealth and scrutiny with more composure than many twice her age might manage. If she enjoys fashion, holidays and the odd extravagance, she is hardly the first bride to take pleasure in a wedding.

What is being held against them, really, is not vulgarity but visibility. They are rich in a way people can see. Their story does not come wrapped in inherited discretion. It comes with photographers outside restaurants, relatives in the papers, friends from home still present, accents unchanged, and no pretence that success has magically made them another species. That is precisely why their marriage has caught the imagination. It is not a royal wedding, but it has a fairytale quality all the same — perhaps a more modern one.

The old fairytales were about princes, castles and bloodlines. The modern British fairytale is different. It is a teenager with a ferocious talent, a childhood sweetheart, a family lifted into a life nobody expected, and a wedding somewhere beautiful, watched by a country that cannot decide whether to cheer or sneer. It is imperfect, certainly. All real fairytales are, once lived by human beings rather than illustrated in books.

No one should confuse sympathy with sainthood. Rooney and McLoughlin are not symbols carved in marble; they are young people making their way through fame, fortune and marriage as best they can. But perhaps that is exactly why the public cruelty feels unnecessary. They have done nothing more outrageous than celebrate their wedding in grand style. In a culture that can be so mean-spirited about joy, that seems a small and forgivable offence.

So let us, for once, resist the urge to turn confetti into ammunition. Let the tabloids count the cost of the flowers if they must. Let the cynics roll their eyes at the setting, the dress, the guest list, the spectacle. The rest of us might simply wish them well.

A boy and a girl from Merseyside have married under the Italian sun. They have known luck, talent, pressure and privilege; they have also known scrutiny most of us would not tolerate for a week. If they have chosen to mark their union with beauty and abundance, good luck to them.

In an age short on romance and long on resentment, Wayne and Coleen’s wedding is not something to mock. It is a reminder that fairytales no longer arrive in glass coaches. Sometimes they come in football boots, childhood loyalty, and a plane to Italy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a long-form entertainment news commentary about the public reaction to Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding, contrasting criticism of their OK magazine deal with Peter Phillips’ Hello magazine deal and highlighting class bias in the coverage.
counterfactuals.output:
# Wayne and Coleen’s Wedding Backlash Says as Much About Britain as It Does About Celebrity Culture

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin married, the public reaction was never just about a footballer, his childhood sweetheart, or a glossy magazine spread. It became a revealing national conversation about money, taste, class, and who is allowed to profit from fame without being sneered at.

Their wedding — lavish, heavily covered, and sold to *OK!* magazine — attracted the kind of commentary that often follows celebrity excess in Britain: tutting about vulgarity, jokes about “chav” culture, and disapproval that a private family moment had been turned into a commercial spectacle. Yet the tone of that criticism looked strikingly different when compared with the response to Peter Phillips, the Queen’s grandson, selling coverage of his wedding to *Hello!* magazine.

Both couples made deals with glossy magazines. Both weddings involved public fascination. Both used access to a private ceremony as a media commodity. But the way each was discussed exposed a familiar double standard: when working-class celebrities cash in, it is often framed as tacky; when the upper classes do the same, it is treated as unfortunate, controversial, or merely a lapse in judgment.

## The Rooney-McLoughlin Wedding as a National Spectacle

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin were never just another celebrity couple. Their relationship had been followed since they were teenagers in Liverpool, long before Coleen became a fashion and lifestyle figure in her own right. Rooney’s rise from Croxteth to Manchester United superstar made him a symbol of modern football wealth: young, working-class, enormously talented, and suddenly richer than most people could imagine.

Coleen, meanwhile, became a tabloid fixture not through aristocratic lineage or theatrical performance, but by virtue of being herself: the girlfriend, then fiancée, then wife of one of England’s most famous footballers. Her shopping trips, holidays, outfits, and friendships became regular fodder for newspapers. She was an early example of a very modern British celebrity — famous through proximity, but also through the public’s own appetite for photographs, gossip, and aspirational consumption.

So when the couple married in Italy and sold the rights to *OK!* magazine, it was hardly surprising. This was the era of big-money celebrity exclusives. Weddings, baby pictures, engagement shoots, home tours — all of it had become part of the fame economy. If newspapers and magazines were already making money from the couple’s image, it was entirely logical that Wayne and Coleen might decide to control the narrative and take the payment themselves.

And yet the reaction was laced with contempt.

Critics mocked the scale of the celebrations, the designer details, the reported cost, and the magazine deal. The implication was not simply that the wedding was expensive, but that it was somehow improperly expensive — too showy, too flashy, too much. The couple’s wealth was treated less as success than as evidence of poor taste.

That distinction matters.

## “Selling Out” or Simply Selling What the Press Already Wanted?

The complaint often made about celebrity magazine deals is that they cheapen a private occasion. A wedding, the argument goes, should be intimate and meaningful, not packaged for public consumption.

There is a fair discussion to be had there. Celebrity culture can blur the line between public interest and personal exploitation. Selling access to private milestones can create a strange performance of intimacy, where readers are invited to feel included in a moment they are actually consuming as a product.

But in the case of Wayne and Coleen, much of the outrage felt selective. They were already being pursued, photographed, judged, and monetised by the media. Paparazzi images of Coleen on holiday or Wayne outside a nightclub were not treated as morally troubling in the same way. Newspapers profited from them constantly. Readers consumed the coverage eagerly.

The moment the couple themselves profited directly from access, however, the moralising began.

That is one of the hypocrisies at the heart of British celebrity coverage. The press often creates the market, feeds the obsession, and then scolds the celebrities for participating in it. The public is encouraged to look, then encouraged to disapprove of what it sees.

## The Peter Phillips Comparison

The contrast with Peter Phillips’ wedding to Autumn Kelly is especially revealing.

Peter Phillips, as the son of Princess Anne and grandson of Queen Elizabeth II, occupied a very different place in the social imagination. He was not a working-class footballer who had become rich through sport. He was part of the extended royal family — not a working royal in the same sense as senior figures, but undeniably connected to the monarchy and all the inherited prestige that comes with it.

When he and Autumn Kelly agreed a deal with *Hello!* magazine for coverage of their wedding, there was controversy. Some critics questioned whether it was appropriate for a royal family member to commercialise access to an event attended by members of the monarchy. Concerns were reportedly raised about the presence of senior royals in a paid magazine spread. The issue was framed around dignity, protocol, and the monarchy’s relationship with commerce.

But the tone was different.

With Peter Phillips, the criticism tended to sound like disappointment that someone from a respected institution had misjudged the optics. With Wayne and Coleen, criticism often carried a sharper edge of ridicule. Their deal was more likely to be discussed in the language of tackiness, excess, and vulgar display.

That difference is the point.

Both deals involved money. Both involved private weddings being turned into glossy content. Yet one was treated as a breach of decorum, while the other was treated as confirmation of low taste.

## Class Bias and the Policing of Taste

Britain has a long history of pretending that class prejudice has softened while continuing to express it through the language of taste.

People may avoid saying openly that they resent working-class people becoming rich, but they will criticise what they buy, how they dress, where they holiday, how they decorate their homes, and how they celebrate. Wealth inherited quietly is often coded as elegance. Wealth earned suddenly is coded as vulgarity.

This is especially true in the treatment of footballers and their partners.

For decades, British footballers have been mocked for having too much money and too little refinement. Their wives and girlfriends — often grouped under the reductive label “WAGs” — have been portrayed as materialistic, fake-tanned, designer-obsessed, and fame-hungry. The label itself became a way of flattening women into accessories: handbags, hair extensions, sunglasses, and shopping bags.

Coleen McLoughlin was frequently viewed through that lens, despite having grown up with Rooney and despite building her own media profile with a degree of shrewdness that critics rarely acknowledged. Her spending was scrutinised in a way that women from aristocratic or old-money backgrounds often avoided. Designer clothes on one woman could be “chic”; on another, “flashy.” A grand wedding in one context could be “traditional”; in another, “tasteless.”

The distinction often came down not to the object itself, but to the class background of the person consuming it.

## The “Vulgarity” Charge

The word that hovers over much of the Rooney-McLoughlin coverage is “vulgar.” It may not always be stated outright, but it is present in the jokes and insinuations: too much money, too much display, too little restraint.

But what is considered vulgar is rarely neutral.

A castle wedding dripping in inherited privilege can be framed as romantic. A society wedding with designer gowns, champagne, and exclusive photographs can be treated as aspirational. Royal pageantry, with its gold carriages, tiaras, uniforms, and balcony appearances, is not exactly modest — yet it is often described as tradition rather than extravagance.

By contrast, a lavish wedding funded by football wages is more likely to be mocked as gaudy.

This is not really about extravagance. It is about who is performing it.

The upper classes are allowed ceremony. The middle classes are allowed “style.” The working classes, when newly wealthy, are accused of showing off.

## Why the Magazine Deals Were Morally Similar

If we strip away the social coding, the Rooney and Phillips magazine deals were fundamentally similar acts: private access exchanged for money and publicity.

One could argue that Peter Phillips’ deal was actually more complicated because of the royal connection. The royal family occupies a constitutional and publicly symbolic role. Even non-senior royals benefit from proximity to taxpayer-funded monarchy, public deference, and institutional prestige. If a royal-adjacent wedding includes senior royals, then selling access raises legitimate questions about whether public status is being converted into private profit.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin, by contrast, were private citizens. Famous, yes. Wealthy, certainly. But their fame came through sport, celebrity media, and public interest — not through constitutional position or hereditary status. If anything, their decision to sell photographs of their wedding was more straightforward. They owned their celebrity image and monetised it in the same marketplace that had long monetised them.

That does not mean everyone had to like the deal. But the moral outrage directed at them often seemed disproportionate when set beside the more measured criticism of Peter Phillips.

## Football Money and British Discomfort

Rooney’s wealth also sat at the centre of the reaction. British culture has an uneasy relationship with football money. Supporters adore footballers on the pitch but often resent their earnings off it. This resentment becomes sharper when players are young, northern, working-class, and visibly wealthy.

Rooney embodied a particular kind of social mobility that Britain both celebrates and mistrusts. He was proof that talent could transform a life. But he also disrupted the old codes around who should have money and how they should behave once they had it.

The criticism of his wedding was therefore about more than a magazine contract. It was about discomfort with a young man from a council-estate background occupying a space of extreme wealth and global attention. It was about the suspicion that he and Coleen had not learned the “right” way to be rich.

But “the right way to be rich” usually means the old way: quietly, securely, with the confidence that comes from never having had to justify it.

## Coleen and the Gendered Dimension

Coleen also bore much of the sneering because women in celebrity culture are often made responsible for the aesthetics of wealth. The footballer may earn the money, but the wife or girlfriend is blamed for how it is displayed.

Coverage of Coleen frequently revolved around clothes, beauty treatments, shopping, and lifestyle. She became a convenient symbol of consumer aspiration, and therefore a convenient target. The wedding deal intensified that dynamic because bridal imagery is already heavily gendered. The dress, the venue, the guests, the flowers, the photographs — all are read as statements about the bride’s taste.

In this sense, criticism of the *OK!* deal was not only classed but gendered. Wayne might be mocked for excess, but Coleen was more likely to be framed as embodying it.

The same scrutiny is not always applied equally to elite women. Aristocratic brides may be discussed in terms of lineage, elegance, and heritage. Celebrity brides from working-class backgrounds are more often evaluated as consumers: what they bought, how much they spent, whether it looked “classy.”

## The Media’s Convenient Amnesia

Another striking element is the media’s tendency to condemn the very celebrity economy it sustains.

Glossy magazines paid for wedding exclusives because they sold copies. Tabloids covered the deals because readers clicked, bought, and argued. Television panels debated the ethics because celebrity weddings were useful content. The outrage itself became profitable.

This is the circular economy of fame: build celebrities up, invade their privacy, encourage public fascination, pay for controlled access, then criticise them for being commercial.

Wayne and Coleen’s wedding was not an aberration. It was a product of its media environment. The only unusual thing was how plainly it exposed the rules. If fame is a market, celebrities will sell. If the public wants access, someone will package it. If newspapers object, they might first ask why they spent so many years training readers to care.

## What the Double Standard Reveals

The comparison between the *OK!* deal and the *Hello!* deal reveals an uncomfortable hierarchy in British public life.

When royalty-adjacent figures commercialise private events, the discussion often centres on propriety. When football celebrities do it, the discussion shifts to taste. One is a question of institutional standards; the other becomes a referendum on personal worth.

That difference is class bias in action.

It is not that Peter Phillips escaped criticism entirely. He did not. His magazine deal caused genuine controversy. But the cultural framing was more forgiving, more formal, and less openly mocking. The assumption seemed to be that he had made an error. With Rooney and Coleen, the assumption was often that they had revealed who they really were.

That is a harsher judgment.

## A Fairer Way to Look at It

A more consistent response would be simple: either we object to all paid wedding exclusives on the grounds that they commodify private life, or we accept that public figures have the right to control and monetise access to their own milestones.

What is harder to defend is objecting more loudly when the people involved are working-class celebrities, while softening the language when similar behaviour comes from people with royal or upper-class connections.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin did not invent celebrity commercialism. They participated in it. Peter Phillips did the same. The difference lay not in the basic transaction, but in how Britain chose to interpret it.

And that interpretation tells us a great deal.

## The Real Story Was Never Just the Wedding

In the end, the public reaction to Wayne and Coleen’s wedding was less about romance than respectability. It asked who gets to be wealthy without apology, who gets to sell access without being demeaned, and who gets to define taste.

The answer, as so often in Britain, seemed to depend on class.

The Rooneys’ wedding was treated by many as a gaudy spectacle; Peter Phillips’ deal as a royal embarrassment. Both were commercial decisions. Both were media events. But only one attracted the full force of Britain’s disdain for newly rich working-class celebrity culture.

That is why the controversy remains interesting years later. It was not merely a celebrity wedding story. It was a mirror held up to a country still deeply invested in class codes, even when it pretends otherwise.

Wayne and Coleen sold their wedding photographs. So did Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly. The deals may have differed in scale, context, and consequence, but the public conversation around them revealed a persistent truth: in British media culture, the act of selling access is judged not only by what is sold, but by who is doing the selling.
